heading: Rules of the Trappists
intro: Trappists follow the Rule of Saint Benedict (6th century), made stricter by Armand de Rancé's reform of 1664. These seven points still shape life in the abbey today.

rules.title: Stabilitas – Stability
rules.text: A monk commits himself for life to a single monastic community, not merely to a place. Benedict of Nursia, Rule ch. 58.

rules.title: Conversatio morum – Conversion of Life
rules.text: The promise of a continual, daily turning towards a simpler life directed towards God – not a single act, but an ongoing process.

rules.title: Oboedientia – Obedience
rules.text: Literally “listening”: obedience to the abbot and the community as an exercise in listening, not mere subordination.

rules.title: Silence
rules.text: Not a strict vow of silence, but a lived restraint: conversation only when necessary. Meals are taken together and in quiet, accompanied by a reading.

rules.title: Manual Labour
rules.text: “Idleness is the enemy of the soul” (Rule, ch. 48). Physical work provides for the community's livelihood and is at the same time a spiritual exercise – crafts such as brewing grew out of it.

rules.title: Simplicity and Penance
rules.text: De Rancé's reform of 1664 tightened the Rule: simple food, abstention from the meat of four-footed animals (fish and poultry are permitted), withdrawal from the world.

rules.title: Divine Office
rules.text: The Liturgy of the Hours – communal prayer several times a day – forms the backbone of the daily routine, around which work and rest are organised.
